regular.can_do: He breaks hard problems into small verified pieces that build on each other. He works alone, checks obsessively, and trusts only what he's proved.
regular.in_the_way: He's trapped in a quiet job that doesn't use him. His best moment today is something nobody asked for and nobody will ever see. And something just happened that doesn't respect small careful steps.
regular.expect_next: An opening that feels like precise literary fiction suddenly cracking into something else—either an accident that matters, or a system intruding on reality. I'm not sure which, but either way I'm waiting to see what he was building and whether he survives the next sentence.

mechanism.can_do: He builds reliable complex systems by breaking them into uncheckable pieces and connecting them carefully, moving methodically without rushing even when people pressure him.
mechanism.in_the_way: He works nights on something nobody asked for, in a low-status job where callers treat him as ridiculous. The best thing in his day is getting two small pieces of his system to work together, and that bothers him less than it should. And then something just happened to the train.
mechanism.expect_next: This is quiet, methodical prose that establishes a pattern of introspection and small victories, then breaks it with something physically wrong. The tilt in that last paragraph was too specific to be scenery. I expect a book about what happens when a system-builder's careful methods meet something that breaks the rules he's been following—or when the rules themselves have changed.

climber.can_do: He can apply systematic biological knowledge to manipulate a magic system that most practitioners treat as intuition, and he's got a companion AI that can read his own body back to him as diagnostic feedback.
climber.in_the_way: He's lost everything and everyone from his old world except the AI. He's trapped in a child's body learning a magic system from first principles while other practitioners treat it as second nature. The biology degree only works as an advantage if the world's magic actually respects that translation.
climber.expect_next: A slow-burn progression story where the appeal is watching him systematically unlock magic through biology instead of talent or innate sensitivity. Academy arc incoming, probably with some friction between his methodical approach and how wizards normally learn. The larger plot lives somewhere downstream of that.

stranger.in_the_way: He wakes up as a child in a place he doesn't understand. He's the only survivor from his world, so he's alone except for an AI that's somehow merged with him in ways that aren't explained. The magic system is complex and learning it is slow.

He'll figure out how biology and magic connect, the merged AI will either become his greatest tool or his biggest problem, and it'll be character-focused rather than action-heavy. The back-cover tells me most of the first act, so the interest is in how it actually plays out, not what happens.

regular.can_do: He can learn magic by treating it as a biology problem, running real-time diagnostics on his own cells while casting. That's a specific enough angle that it actually gives him an edge, rather than just making him smart in a generic way.
regular.in_the_way: He's starting over as a child with no context, no home language probably, no social standing. Everything is new except the AI voice in his head and his memory of how living things work. The AI is all he has left but also the thing that makes him alien to this world.
regular.expect_next: A progression fantasy academy story where he slowly figures out the rules of magic by treating it like cellular biology. The premise promises system-building rather than just hand-waving, which means I'm expecting to actually *learn* something alongside him, the way Mother of Learning does it. Whether it delivers on that or just uses the biology framing as window dressing is the test.
